questions.q_en: Which Supreme Court case established that the 'procedure established by law' must be "fair, just and reasonable"?
options_en: A.K. Gopalan vs. State of Madras
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Shankari Prasad v. Union of India
questions.solution_en:
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India

· In this landmark case (1978), the Supreme Court overturned its earlier view in A.K. Gopalan case and held that the "procedure established by law" under Article 21 must be "fair, just and reasonable."

· This case significantly expanded the scope of Article 21 and established that fundamental rights cannot be read in isolation but must be read together as they form an integrated scheme.

questions.q_en: In which case did the Supreme Court first establish that Parliament's power to amend the Constitution does not extend to altering its 'basic structure'?
questions.solution_en:
· In 1973, the 13-judge bench in Kesavananda Bharati case established the 'Basic Structure Doctrine'.

· While the Court held that Parliament could amend any part of the Constitution, it could not alter its basic structure.

· This remains one of the most significant constitutional decisions that limited Parliament's amending powers.

questions.q_en: Which fundamental right formed the basis of Supreme Court's judgment in striking down the Electoral Bonds Scheme in 2024?
questions.solution_en:
The Supreme Court struck down the Electoral Bonds Scheme primarily on the grounds that it violated voters' right to know about political funding, which is an essential aspect of freedom of expression under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.

Two unanimous verdicts were delivered by a five-judge bench headed by Chief Justice of India DY Chandrachud.

What Is Article 19 (1)(a)

· Article 19 (1)(a) in the Constitution of India guarantees all citizens the "right to freedom of speech and expression". Under this, an Indian citizen has been granted the right to freely express his/her opinions, ideas and thoughts.

· It also provides citizens the freedom to express their views through writing, speech, visual representations, and printing among other means.

What Is Electoral Bonds Scheme

· The electoral bonds scheme was notified by the central government on January 2, 2018, as an alternative to cash donations made to political parties.

· It was stated that the scheme was a part of efforts to bring transparency to political funding.

· Electoral bonds may be purchased by any Indian citizen or entity incorporated or established in the country, as per the provisions of the scheme.

· These electoral bonds can be purchased by an individual either singly or jointly with others.

questions.q_en: The foundation case for Public Interest Litigation in India is considered to be:
questions.solution_en:
The foundation case for Public Interest Litigation (PIL) in India is considered to be the (1) Mumbai Kamgar Sabha case (1976).

In this case, the Supreme Court relaxed the traditional rule of locus standi (the requirement that only an aggrieved party can file a case) and allowed a trade union to file a petition on behalf of workers. This marked the beginning of the PIL movement in India, enabling courts to address issues of public importance and protect the rights of marginalized groups.

The other cases mentioned are :

· Sunil Batra case: Dealt with prisoner rights and conditions in jails.

· Bandhua Mukti Morcha case: Focused on bonded labor and workers' rights.

· Vishaka case: Laid down guidelines to prevent sexual harassment at the workplace.

questions.q_en:

A. First Judges Case1. Established 5-member collegium
B. Second Judges Case2. Struck down NJAC
C. Third Judges Case3. Government's primacy in appointments
D. Fourth Judges Case4. CJI's primacy in appointments
questions.solution_en:
· The First Judges Case, 1981, held that the President (executive) had primacy in judicial appointments, with limited consultation with the judiciary.

· The Second Judges Case, 1993, established the collegium system, giving primacy to the Chief Justice of India (CJI) in judicial appointments, with consultation with senior judges.

· The Third Judges Case, 1998, expanded the collegium to a 5-member body (CJI + 4 senior-most judges) for judicial appointments and transfers.

· The Fourth Judges Case, 2015, struck down the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC), reaffirming the collegium system as the method for judicial appointments.

questions.q_en: What was the key principle laid down by the Supreme Court while upholding Section 6A of Citizenship Act regarding Assam?
options_en: Cultural identity cannot override constitutional provisions
Migration concerns must be balanced with humanitarian considerations
Implementation issues don't make the law unconstitutional
State's powers in citizenship matters are absolute
questions.solution_en:
· While upholding Section 6A of the Citizenship Act regarding Assam, the Court emphasized that problems in implementation cannot make a law unconstitutional.

· The Court recognized Assam's distinct identity while upholding the constitutional validity of the provision.

· In the case of Assam Sanmilita Mahasangha v. Union of India (2014), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of Section 6A of the Citizenship Act, which was inserted by the 1985 Assam Accord to address the issue of illegal migrants in Assam.

· The court ruled that implementation challenges (such as difficulties in identifying and deporting illegal migrants) do not render the law itself unconstitutional. However, the court also emphasized the need for effective implementation and monitoring.

questions.q_en: Under which Article of the Constitution did the Supreme Court establish the collegium system in the Second Judges Case?
questions.solution_en:
· The Supreme Court established the collegium system in the Second Judges Case (1993) under Article 124 of the Indian Constitution.

· Article 124 deals with the appointment of judges to the Supreme Court and provides the framework for judicial appointments.

· In the Second Judges Case, the Supreme Court interpreted this article to give primacy to the Chief Justice of India (CJI) in the appointment process, requiring consultation with a collegium of senior judges.

· This marked the beginning of the collegium system.

The other articles mentioned are:

· Article 217: Deals with the appointment of High Court judges.

· Article 141: States that the law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts in India.

· Article 142: Grants the Supreme Court the power to pass any order necessary for doing complete justice.
